paras.text: Michigan Licensing Law and Exam Logistics — Audio Lecture

Welcome to the licensing law chapter. This is the single biggest business and law category on your exam. Out of fifty business and law questions, thirteen come from regulatory and statutory requirements — more than one in four. And unlike code questions, there is nothing to interpret here. It is pure memorization of Michigan law. Every question you lock down in this chapter is a nearly free point on exam day. Let's earn all thirteen.

First, the big picture. Michigan licenses residential builders under Article twenty four of the Occupational Code. That's Public Act two ninety nine of nineteen eighty, sections M C L three thirty nine point two four zero one through two four one two. The program is run by LARA — the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs — through its Bureau of Construction Codes. There is also a board: the Residential Builders and Maintenance and Alteration Contractors Board, with nine members. Four licensed residential builders, two licensed M and A contractors, and three members of the public.

Now the definitions, because the exam loves them. A residential structure, under the current statute, is one of two things. A detached one or two family dwelling, or a townhouse of not more than three stories above grade plane with a separate means of egress. Say that again to yourself. Detached one or two family, or a townhouse, three stories or less, separate egress. This definition was rewritten in twenty twenty, so older study materials that talk about combination residential and commercial structures are out of date. If an answer choice says any building of three units or less, that is a trap. Unit count alone is not the test.

A residential builder is anyone who, for compensation other than wages for personal labor only, undertakes or even offers to undertake construction, repair, alteration, improvement, wrecking, or demolition of a residential structure. Notice — offering counts. You can violate the licensing law without ever driving a nail. The definition also sweeps in people who deal in prefabricated, precut, packaged, or shell housing, and anyone who erects a residential structure except on their own property for their own use and occupancy.

The maintenance and alteration contractor — the M and A license — covers repair, alteration, additions, improvement, wrecking, building a garage, and laying concrete on residential property. It also catches house flippers. If you buy, substantially rehab, and resell the same residential structure more than twice in one calendar year, you need a license — unless it's for your own use and occupancy, or you hire all the work out to licensed contractors. Remember the relationship: a residential builder license covers everything the M and A license covers, but an M and A contractor cannot do new construction.

A salesperson is an employee or agent, other than a qualifying officer, of a licensed builder or contractor, who sells or solicits contracts for the licensee's services. Occasional and incidental sales don't count.

Now, when do you not need a license at all? The exemptions in section two four zero three. Government representatives. An owner building on their own property for their own use and occupancy. An owner of rental property doing maintenance and alteration of that rental property. Officers of a court. Subcontractors working solely under contract with a licensed builder. Licensed electrical, plumbing, and mechanical contractors — but only for their own trade work. And the famous six hundred dollar exemption: if the aggregate price for labor, materials, and everything else on one undertaking is less than six hundred dollars, no license is required. But watch the anti-evasion clause — you cannot split a big job into little contracts under six hundred dollars to dodge the act. If the work is part of a larger operation, the exemption is gone. And remember what six hundred dollars is not: it is not a written contract trigger. It is purely a licensure exemption threshold.

Two more framework facts. Michigan does not license commercial builders at the state level — Article twenty four is residential only. And Michigan has no reciprocity with any other state. An out of state builder starts from scratch here.

How do you get the license? Four things. Good moral character — and for a company, that reaches every partner, officer, director, member, and shareholder. Proof of identity — a copy of your driver's license or state I D, which the department may use only to prove identity. The sixty hour prelicensure education. And the exam. Notice what is not on the list: experience. The statute has no experience requirement.

The sixty hour course has been required since June first, two thousand eight, and it must include at least six hours in each of seven competency areas. Here they are. Business management, estimating, and job costing. Design and building science. Contracts, liability, and risk management. Marketing and sales. Project management and scheduling. The current Michigan residential code. And MIOSHA construction safety standards. Seven areas, six hours minimum each, sixty hours total. And a nice detail: the certificate never expires, as long as the course was taken after June first, two thousand eight.

One deadline that trips people up: once LARA receives your application, you have one year to complete everything, including passing the exam. Miss the year and your fees are forfeited and the application is void.

The license itself runs for three years. You must maintain a place of business in Michigan, and every additional location needs a branch office license. Nonresidents must file a consent to service of process. And your contracts must include your license information — your individual license, and any license you hold as a qualifying officer of a company.

Renewal. When you renew, you state two things to the department: that you have a current copy of the Michigan Residential Code, and that you meet your continuing competency requirements. Keep your continuing education documentation for at least five years. The hours depend on when you were first licensed. Licensed on or after January first, two thousand nine? Twenty one hours per three year cycle, including at least three hours every calendar year during your first six years, with at least three hours on codes, safety, and changes in the law. Licensed before two thousand nine with a clean record? Just three hours per cycle — one hour of codes, one hour of safety, one hour of legal issues. And if you get disciplined, the department can order anywhere from three to twenty one hours in the next cycle.

If your license lapses, here's the ladder. Expired less than three years — application and a one hundred eighty five dollar fee, and you're back. Lapsed more than three years — you start over: sixty hours of prelicensure again, application, fees, good moral character, and you retake the exam.

Companies. A corporation, partnership, or L L C is a new legal person and needs its own license. It designates a qualifying officer from its officers, partners, members, or managing agent. The qualifying officer passes the exam and must also obtain and maintain their own individual license. The qualifying officer is responsible for supervising and controlling the construction operations to secure compliance with the law. Everyone with control in the entity must be at least eighteen. Now the suspension chains — these make great exam questions. If the qualifying officer's license is suspended, revoked, or denied, the company's license is suspended. If the qualifying officer leaves the company, the company license is suspended, though the department can allow a reasonable time to qualify a replacement. And a licensee on inactive status cannot serve as a qualifying officer.

Discipline. A homeowner has eighteen months to file a complaint. Eighteen months from the latest of completion, occupancy, or purchase for a maintenance and alteration job, or from the certificate of occupancy or closing for a project that needs an occupancy permit. The list of conduct that gets you disciplined is long, but the greatest hits are: abandonment of a project without legal excuse. Diversion of funds — taking money for one project and spending it on another. Failure to account for money belonging to others. Willful departure from the plans and specifications without consent. Willful violation of building laws. Failing to notify the department within ten days of a change in the control of the business. Failing to deliver the entire agreement to the purchaser. Aiding and abetting an unlicensed person, or lending out your license. Becoming insolvent or filing bankruptcy. And here's one people don't expect — workmanship that doesn't meet the Michigan Residential Code is itself a discipline ground, all by itself.

For workmanship complaints there's a special procedure. The homeowner sends the department a written complaint and a copy to the builder at the same time. You are presumed innocent until the hearing examiner finds otherwise. Once a building inspection report verifies the complaint, the department must mail you the verified complaint by certified mail within thirty days, or it loses the ability to fine you — although it can still pursue restitution or suspension. And builders can put an alternative dispute resolution clause in their contracts. If a complainant skips your contractual A D R procedure and sues, that failure is an affirmative defense.

Penalties. Learn these in three buckets. Bucket one, administrative — what LARA itself can do: limit, suspend, deny, or revoke your license, censure, probation, restitution, and an administrative fine of up to ten thousand dollars. Bucket two, criminal — for unlicensed residential building, the fines run five thousand to twenty five thousand dollars. First offense, a misdemeanor with up to one year. Second offense, up to two years. And if the unlicensed work causes death or serious injury, it becomes a felony with up to four years. Bucket three, civil — the attorney general or a prosecutor can sue, and the court shall assess a civil fine of five thousand to twenty five thousand dollars on top of any damages.

And the hammer that matters most in real life: an unlicensed builder cannot sue to collect payment. Section two four one two. You must allege and prove you were licensed during the performance of the work. No license, no lawsuit, and no construction lien either. One trap to bury forever: there is no such statute as M C L three thirty nine point six one one. The penalty sections are six zero one, six zero two, and two four one two.

Now exam logistics. PSI administers the test. One hundred sixty questions. Fifty business and law, one hundred ten trade. You need one hundred sixteen correct — seventy two and a half percent. You get two hundred forty minutes. Closed book. Since November fourteenth, twenty nineteen, it is one combined exam with one score — no separate section passes, and if you fail, you retake the whole thing. Up to ten unscored experimental questions may be mixed in. The trade questions reference the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code — confirmed current in the PSI handbook updated August of twenty twenty six. Fees: one hundred ninety five dollars to apply to LARA, one hundred seventeen dollars for the exam, and the same for a retest. The salesperson exam is forty five questions, thirty two to pass, ninety minutes, eighty five dollars, with no education requirement. Practical rules: no walk-ins. Cancel at least two days ahead or lose your fee. Arrive thirty minutes early — show up after the start time and you forfeit. Bring one valid signature-bearing photo I D matching your registration name. Your calculator must be silent, battery powered, non printing, with no alphabet keys — and the measurement-converting construction calculators are banned. If you pass, you only see the word pass. If you fail, you get section scores. There is no post-exam review.

Time for the rapid fire recap. Article twenty four, Public Act two ninety nine of nineteen eighty. Nine board members — four builders, two M and A, three public. Residential structure — detached one or two family, or townhouse of three stories or less with separate egress. Six hundred dollars — licensure exemption, aggregate price, anti-splitting rule. Sixty hours prelicensure, seven areas, six hours each, effective June first, two thousand eight, certificate never expires. One year to finish licensure after applying. License term, three years. Continuing competency — twenty one hours per cycle if licensed after two thousand nine, three hours per year in the first six years; three hours per cycle if licensed before. Keep records five years. Twelve M and A crafts. Entity principals at least eighteen. Complaint window, eighteen months. Change of control notice, ten days. Verified complaint certified mail, thirty days. Administrative fine, ten thousand max. Criminal and civil fines, five to twenty five thousand. Jail — one year first offense, two years second, four years felony if death or serious injury. No license means no lawsuit and no lien. Exam — one sixty questions, fifty business and law, one ten trade, one sixteen to pass, two forty minutes, closed book, combined since November twenty nineteen. Regulatory and statutory requirements — thirteen questions. Insurance, bonds and liens — eleven. Fees — one ninety five application, one seventeen exam, one eighty five relicensure, eighty five salesperson. And the code on the exam is the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code.
That's the chapter. Thirteen questions, all sitting right here. Drill the numbers until they're automatic, and go take them.
